text:
In a rough comparison to Bitcoin Core, their one repo embeds both leveldb (3rd party dependency) and libsecp256k1 (which we also use but don't embed). They also implement a full wallet. While we have wallet code in system, our comparable client interface code is in explorer, and isn't a wallet, and BC has common code for wallet shared with the node as well. So I use this filter to count its loc:
`cpp,.hpp,.c,.h,.ipp,.cc,!secp256k1,!wallet,!leveldb`

Which comes out to `240,172` - most directly comparable to our `251,056`, which excludes all build artifacts in both cases. If you include its `/wallet` directory and our explorer, it's `270,907` loc of code to our 251,056 + 48,009 = `299,065`. Roughly speaking, libbitcoin is about 10% more loc in c/c++ than Bitcoin Core. In some ways we have more functionality (e.g. Electrum server), and others we have less (e.g. no tx pool).

In the last couple days I've completed most of the alternate json serializations for bitcoind (and by pass-thru, electrum) objects. The generalization makes it easy to add other forms as well. It's mostly just another set of annotations over the objects, just needed a context to hang that on. I've left out of the static object serializations anything that is not a property or computable from properties of the objects. In other words state that is out of context (there is a bunch of this in bitcoind objects). That just gets injected (e.g. by the server) into the JSON DOM after it's constructed from a chain class instance.

elements.text:
Hi all. This is Adi, program lead at Summer of Bitcoin - a non-profit that runs a global internship program for university students to work on bitcoin open-source software.

In 2024, Tanay and Shashank contributed to libbitcoin under the Summer of Bitcoin internship program. We'd love to have libbitcoin again this year!

What’s different this year: AI has made "starting" a hundred ideas easy. The bottleneck is still shipping - correctness, tests, benchmarks, reviewability, docs, and getting changes into the hands of real users. This year's application process was geared towards selecting interns who use AI as a force multiplier but can still do the hard last-mile work to get something safely merged and actually adopted.
Project ideas can be classic (core dev / infra / testing / performance / DevEx), but we’re also explicitly excited about AI-native directions like:
agent-facing interfaces (e.g., MCP/tool-style APIs) so dev agents can discover and use the project
UX/UI + design research work to make things easier for end users and developers
fun/peripheral/risky-exploratory prototypes - as long as they still ship durable artifacts (tests + docs + demo)

In brief: mentors propose 1–3 project ideas, candidates submit detailed proposals, you select the best fit, and SoB pays those selected with a stipend in BTC. If you’re open to it, I’m happy to share more details!

elements.text: I've verified blocks-out (and headers out) against a local core v28.0 node. Had one initial issue (an inverted operator), but then kept having what appeared to be race conditions. After digging into it, it turns out core is sending overlapping
getdata

(block) requests. I verified this on our end but also in their code.

Since we have to deal with them, we have to treat this as allowed behavior. So I made it configurable. You'll be able to watch the overlapped I/O errors cause core nodes to drop by changing config

. Working well now, passing block 375k on one manual connection from core, with no drops or delays.

I'm perf-logging our block retrieval time, and had to change the scale to microseconds. Adding up all times the total retrieval time is 29% of the total time. If core took the same time to read and serialize the block as we took to deserialize and write it, the run at that point (300k, or ~5% of the chain) would be 15 minutes, but it's about 53 minutes. This machine syncs the entire chain off the Internet in 53 minutes.

text:
I've verified blocks-out (and headers out) against a local core v28.0 node. Had one initial issue (an inverted operator), but then kept having what appeared to be race conditions. After digging into it, it turns out core is sending overlapping `getdata` (block) requests. I verified this on our end but also in their code.

Since we have to deal with them, we have to treat this as allowed behavior. So I made it configurable. You'll be able to watch the overlapped I/O errors cause core nodes to drop by changing config :slightly_smiling_face:. Working well now, passing block 375k on one manual connection from core, with no drops or delays.

I'm perf-logging our block retrieval time, and had to change the scale to microseconds. Adding up all times the total retrieval time is 29% of the total time. If core took the same time to read and serialize the block as we took to deserialize and write it, the run at that point (300k, or ~5% of the chain) would be 15 minutes, but it's about 53 minutes. This machine syncs the entire chain off the Internet in 53 minutes.

elements.text: There were early claims by some people that our indexed block storage would result in long block query times, slowing IBD. This was predictably not true, because writing is more costly than reading, and we write easily the entire store in 45 minutes. But this just reinforces that fact. Even with full block object reconstruction from the relational store, where each op in each script is stored as an object with a shared pointer (for push data), and then wire serialization from that object model, it is much faster than necessary. And reducing the query to just construct the wire serialization directly will easily cut this in half.

elements.text: I spent yesterday implementing the direct translation from the store for header, block, and tx, into wire serialization. The low level store getters are provided a stream reader, so I just pass in a stream writer reference with the getters and read directly into the output stream. Since the writer is just an interface the caller can pass in a hex stream writer, which allows for streaming directly to hex (text) for the interfaces that require it (like electrum/bitcoind json-rpc). We could also pass a socket writer reference and pass directly from the store into the socket buffer.

elements.text: Just completed the optimized block (and tx/header) wire serialization queries and hook into the block-out protocol. So instead of populating a block object and serializing it, we are reading it directly from the store into wire serialization, and copying it into the write buffer. Savings in query time in the first 125k blocks is about 28%. These are tiny blocks, so I didn't expect to see much change. So instead of populating a block object and serializing it, we are reading it directly from the store into wire serialization, and copying it into the write buffer. Savings in query time in the first 125k blocks is about 28%. These are tiny blocks, so I didn't expect to see much change. As they get 3 orders of magnitude larger the savings should go up dramatically. Mind you, it was already fast :slightly_smiling_face:.

Right is manually connecting on ipv4 and ipv6 for localhost and two physical adapters (6 connections). Left has 100 outbound and 100 inbound connections enabled as well. Also running a core node connected via manual localhost. Left is just pumping blocks and other message traffic and Right is balancing work across 6 channels. Allowed deviation (sd) is set to zero on Left, so no dropping of slow/stalled connections (optimal given all are against the same process).
